{{Short description|Mathematical concept}}
{{Distinguish|Dedekind ring}}
In [[mathematics]], a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] is said to be a '''Dedekind-finite ring''' (also called '''directly finite rings'''<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Goodearl |first=Kenneth |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5FKzb7LZMvAC&dq=%22directly+finite+rings%22&pg=PA166 |title=Ring Theory: Nonsingular Rings and Modules |date=1976 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-0-8247-6354-1 |pages=165–166 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Breaz" /><ref name="Riis" /> and '''Von Neumann finite rings'''<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Lam |first=T. Y. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2PwGCAAAQBAJ |title=A First Course in Noncommutative Rings |date=2012-12-06 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-1-4684-0406-7 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Breaz" /><ref name="Riis" />) if ''ab'' = 1 implies ''ba'' = 1 for any two ring elements ''a'' and ''b''. In other words, all one-sided inverses in the ring are two-sided. Numerous examples of Dedekind-finite rings include [[commutative rings]], [[finite rings]], and [[Noetherian rings]].

== Definitions ==

A ring <math>R</math> is Dedekind-finite if any of the following equivalent conditions hold:<ref name="Riis">{{citation|last1=Riis |first1=Søren |title=Network Communication with operators in Dedekind Finite and Stably Finite Rings |date=5 July 2015 |arxiv=1507.01249 }}</ref>{{better source needed|date=June 2025}}
* All one sided inverses are two sided: <math>xy = 1</math> implies <math>yx = 1</math>.
* Each element that has a right inverse has a left inverse: For <math>x \in R</math>, if there is a <math>y \in R</math> where <math>xy = 1</math>, then there is a <math>z \in R</math> such that <math>zx = 1</math>.
* Capacity condition: <math>xy=1</math>, <math>xz=0</math> implies <math>z=0</math>.
* Each element has at most one right inverse.
* Each element that has a left inverse has a right inverse.
* Dual of the capacity condition: <math>yx=1</math>, <math>zx=0</math> implies <math>z=0</math>.
* Each element has at most one left inverse.
* Each element that has a right inverse also has a two sided inverse.

== Examples ==

* Any [[commutative ring]] is Dedekind-finite.<ref name="Riis" />
* Any [[finite ring]] is Dedekind-finite.<ref name=":1" />
* Any [[matrix ring]] <math>M_n(F)</math> over a commutative ring <math>F</math> is Dedekind-finite.<ref name="Riis" />
* Any [[domain (ring theory)|domain]] is Dedekind-finite.<ref name=":1" />
* Any left/right [[Noetherian ring]] is Dedekind-finite.<ref name=":1" /><ref name="Riis" />
* Given a [[Group (mathematics)|group]] <math>G</math>, the [[group ring|group algebra]] <math>kG</math> is Dedekind-finite.<ref name="Riis" />
* A Dedekind-finite ring with an [[Idempotent (ring theory)|idempotent]] <math>e^2=e</math> implies that the [[corner ring]] <math>eRe</math> is also Dedekind-finite.<ref name="Breaz" />
* A ring with finitely many [[Nilpotent|nilpotents]] is Dedekind-finite.<ref name="Riis" />
* A [[Von Neumann regular ring#Generalizations and specializations|unit-regular ring]] is Dedekind-finite.<ref name=":1" />

== Non-examples ==

A counter-example can be constructed by considering the [[free algebra]] <math>R\langle x,y\rangle</math> (a "[[polynomial ring]]" in two non-commuting indeterminates, that is, <math>xy \neq yx</math>), where the ring <math>R</math> has no [[zero divisors]], being divided by the [[Ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] <math>I=(xy-1)</math>. Then <math>x+I \in R\langle x,y\rangle/I</math> has a right inverse but is not invertible. This illustrates that Dedekind-finite rings need not be closed under [[Ring homomorphism|homomorpic images]].<ref name="Breaz" />

Another non-example is the [[endomorphism ring]] <math>\operatorname{End}(V)</math> of a [[vector space]] (or [[free module]]) <math>V</math> with a countably infinite basis <math>e_1,e_2,\dots</math>. Let <math>L\in\operatorname{End}(V)</math> be the left [[Shift_operator#Sequences|shift]] defined by <math>L(e_1)=0</math> and <math>L(e_i)=e_{i-1}</math> for <math>i\geq2</math>, and let <math>R\in\operatorname{End}(V)</math> be the right shift <math>R(e_i)=e_{i+1}</math>. Then <math>LR=1</math>, but <math>RL(e_1)=0</math>.<ref name=":1" />

A matrix ring over a Dedekind-finite ring may also fail to be Dedekind-finite. For this, one can consider <math>R=k\langle s,t,u,v,w,x,y,z\rangle</math>, where <math>k</math> is a field, let <math>A=\begin{pmatrix}s&t\\u&v\end{pmatrix}</math>, <math>B=\begin{pmatrix}w&x\\y&z\end{pmatrix}</math>, and <math>J</math> the two-sided ideal of <math>R</math> generated by the entries of <math>AB-I</math>. Then <math>R/J</math> is a domain, but <math>AB=I\ne BA</math> in <math>M_2(R/J)</math>.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Lam | first1=Tsit-Yuen | author-link=Tsit Yuen Lam | title=Exercises in modules and rings | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | location=Berlin, New York | series=Problem Books in Mathematics | isbn=978-0-387-98850-4| mr=2278849 | year=2007 | zbl=1121.16001 |page=11 }}</ref>

== Properties ==

Dedekind-finite rings are closed under [[Subring|subrings]]<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Breaz">{{citation|last1=Breaz |first1=Simion |last2=Călugăreanu |first2=Grigore |last3=Schultz |first3=Phill |title=Modules with Dedekind Finite Endomorphism Rings}}</ref>{{better source needed|date=June 2025}}, [[Direct product|direct products]],<ref name="Riis" /><ref name="Breaz" /> and finite [[Direct sum|direct sums]].<ref name="Breaz" /> This makes the class of Dedekind-finite rings a [[quasivariety]], which can also be seen from the fact that its axioms are [[equations]] and the [[Horn sentence]] <math>ab=1 \implies ba=1</math>.<ref name="Breaz" /> 

A ring is Dedekind-finite if and only if so is its [[opposite ring]].<ref name="Breaz" /> If either a ring <math>R</math>, its [[polynomial ring]] <math>R[X] </math> with indeterminates <math>X</math>, the [[free word algebra]] <math>R[\tilde{X}]</math> over <math>X</math> with coefficients in <math>R</math>, or the [[power series ring]] <math>R[[X]]</math> are Dedekind-finite, then they all are Dedekind-finite.<ref name="Breaz" /> Letting <math>\text{Rad}(R)</math> denote the [[Jacobson radical]] of the ring <math>R</math>, the [[quotient ring]] <math>R/\text{Rad}(R)</math> is Dedekind-finite if and only if so is <math>R</math>, and this implies that [[local rings]] and [[Semi-local ring|semilocal rings]] are also Dedekind-finite.<ref name="Breaz" /> This extends to the fact that, given a ring <math>R</math> and a [[nilpotent ideal]] <math>I</math>, the ring <math>R</math> is Dedekind-finite [[if and only if]] so is the quotient ring <math>R/I</math>,<ref name="Breaz" /> and as a consequence, a ring is also Dedekind-finite if and only if the [[upper triangular matrices]] with coeffecients in the ring also form a Dedekind-finite ring.<ref name="Breaz" />
